intro: Pachmann recorded the D-flat nocturne on his own Baldwin piano at Hayes on26 June 1925. The December 1925 Gramophone review names HMV DB 860 and remarks that, despite his talkative reputation, he does not speak on the disc. This transfer preserves that issued performance rather than a later retelling of his mannerisms.
question: What remains of Pachmann’s style without spoken theatrics?

cues.title: He does not speak
cues.text: The contemporary reviewer explicitly noted the absence of spoken comments on DB 860. Listen to the musical phrasing itself, not the anecdotes often attached to Pachmann’s name.

cues.title: An early recorded crest
cues.text: The transfer’s highest five-second average level falls in this early expansion. Later strong passages do not simply outgrow it in recorded amplitude.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-nocturne-op27-2-pachmann-1925.txt: highest level60 seconds; other high windows135, 140, 145, 205 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: A strong internal turn
cues.text: The analysis finds a very strong change here and another around 2:38. Compare the flow between these landmarks with Lévy’s longer recording; the measured boundary does not identify a particular ornament.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-nocturne-op27-2-pachmann-1925.txt: near-equal maximum novelty130 and158 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: Sonority through a 1925 review
cues.text: The Gramophone reviewer praised the performance’s spirit while noting uneven recorded piano sonority. Apparent clang and balance in this transfer cannot all be assigned to the pianist’s touch.

cues.title: The final withdrawal
cues.text: The ending falls into a much quieter region. Listen to how the line winds down rather than reading the transfer’s crackle as continuing keyboard activity.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
